drills.q: What is the cell count for a full factorial design with 3 factors at 2 levels each?
drills.a: 2^3 = 8 cells, each needing roughly the same per-arm sample size as a standalone A/B test.

drills.q: How is sample ratio mismatch (SRM) detected?
drills.a: A chi-squared goodness-of-fit test comparing observed vs expected traffic split between arms, commonly triggered at p < 0.001.

drills.q: Derive/compute: baseline conversion 5%, want to detect a 10% relative lift, alpha=0.05 two-sided, 80% power. Roughly how many visitors per arm?
Why does halving the MDE roughly quadruple the required sample size?
drills.a: The effect size (p2-p1) is squared in the denominator of the sample size formula, so halving it multiplies the required n by roughly 4x.

drills.q: Explain CUPED and derive why it reduces variance.
drills.a: Y_cuped = Y - theta*(X-E[X]), theta = Cov(X,Y)/Var(X), using a pre-experiment covariate X unaffected by treatment. From OLS variance algebra, Var(Y_cuped) = Var(Y)*(1-rho^2), so a covariate correlated at rho=0.7 with the outcome cuts variance ~51%.

drills.q: A triggered SRM check coincides with a treatment arm that looks significantly better. Do you trust the result?
drills.a: No. SRM invalidates the causal comparison until root-caused -- the missing/excess users are systematically, not randomly, different, so the headline result is unreliable even if it looks convincing.

drills.q: Why does a network-effect-sensitive feature (e.g. referrals) require cluster randomization rather than user-level randomization?
drills.a: Even at user-level randomization, a treated user's action (sharing/referring) can affect a control user, leaking the treatment's effect across arms. Cluster randomization (by friend-group or geo-market) contains spillover within one arm.

drills.q: Your team wants a 3-factor MVT (headline x image x CTA color) with only 15,000 visitors/week. Design the study.
drills.a: Compute cell count (e.g. 2^3=8) and per-cell sample size needed for the acceptable MDE; compare to available traffic over a reasonable duration. If it doesn't fit, propose a half-fraction fractional factorial (4 cells, aliasing the 3-way interaction with a factor judged implausible to interact), or test the two most-likely-to-interact factors as a full 2x2 and the third sequentially. Show the traffic math explicitly rather than running an underpowered design.

drills.q: Walk through the pipeline stages where SRM can originate and how you'd root-cause a triggered check.
drills.a: Assignment (bucketing bugs, ID collisions), execution (a variant's own bug, often JS, breaking tracking/redirect), logging (asymmetric join dropping rows by arm), analysis (asymmetric post-hoc filter). Root-cause stage by stage starting from raw assignment-service bucket counts before any downstream filtering, then check for elevated error rates or missing events specifically in the affected arm.

drills.q: A stakeholder says the test showed 'no significant difference' and concludes the treatment has no effect. Why is that not the same claim, and what should you report instead?
drills.a: A null result only rules out effects larger than the test's actual MDE at the collected sample size; it says nothing about smaller, still-meaningful effects. Report the achieved MDE alongside any null result and phrase the conclusion as 'we can rule out an effect larger than X%' rather than 'no effect.'
